sentences.text: This animal was a long-legged bird with short wings and a large skull, resembling the shape of phorusrhacids. Its species varied in size, ranging from those comparable to modern seriemas to individuals reaching two meters in length.
It possessed a highly reduced first toe and a robust jugal, features that may have evolved convergently with phorusrhacids.
The genus was named "tall bird" because it was significantly larger than its modern seriema relatives.
Bathornis is the most species-rich genus among all Cariamiformes, whether extinct or extant.
The specific species name "veredus" is a Latin word relating to speed, though its exact etymological explanation was not provided.
The genus Bathornis was named by Wetmore in 1927.
Storrs Olson reassigned fossils originally interpreted as a terrestrial vulture to Bathornis in 1985.
Bathornis was a flightless predator that occupied niches typically dominated by mammals. It was a carnivorous bird.
Bathornis grallator and B. veredus had strong beaks similar to phorusrhacids, with identical jugal reinforcement indicating similar biting stresses.
Large Bathornis species were likely apex predators that competed successfully with mammals for over 17 million years.
The presence of Bathornis species near large mammals like Megacerops and Merycoidodon might indicate they preyed on them.
Bathornis shared its habitat with carnivorous mammals such as hyaenodontids, entelodonts, and nimravids, and competed with the bird Paracrax.
There may be evidence that Bathornis and Paracrax avoided direct competition by living in different environments, with Paracrax in drier areas.
Bathornis lived in various environments because of its long existence and many species.
Bathornis belongs to the family Bathornithidae.
The type species of the genus Bathornis is Bathornis veredus.
Bathornis lived from the Lutetian to the Burdigalian stages, between 45.9 and 18.5 million years ago.
The known range of Bathornis was located around the area that is now the Great Plains.
A recent study suggests Bathornis is the sole representative of Bathornithidae, placing it outside the clade containing seriemas and phorusrhacids.
A 2024 study finds Bathornis closer to seriemas than to phorusrhacids.
Researchers caution that some sympatric Bathornis species might represent different sexes or morphs rather than distinct species.
Recent analyses suggest that Bathornis likely preferred wetland environments.
